A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VFF/V3 research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original super-resolution experiments, including PSNR/SSIM, temporal consistency, computational requirements and appendix evaluations of V2.5.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, basis analyses, ablations and input-corruption experiments.

M1.justification: The RVRT-conditioned local Fourier representation, globally learned frequencies and PSF-aware sampling remain unchanged. V3-Large and V2.5 already appear in v1. Specifying the L1 reconstruction loss in v2 documents an existing training objective rather than establishing a method change.

E1.justification: Adobe240, GoPro, Vid4 and REDS remain the datasets, with the same principal super-resolution tasks. v2 extends input conditions through Gaussian-noise and noise-plus-H.264 tests on Vid4 (Appendix B.4), alongside a selected camera-motion-blur example in Figure 13.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds RDN-HIIF to the image-super-resolution comparators. Appendix B.2 and Table 7 introduce a separate comparison against BasicVSR, TTVSR and FTVSR, substantially broadening the evaluated competitor families. The V2.5 comparison against SAVSR, B-AVSR and ST-AVSR already existed in v1.

E3.justification: New controlled experiments vary basis size from 128 to 768, compare learned and fixed frequencies, and evaluate 25% and 50% training budgets. Appendix B.4 adds five noise levels, with and without H.264 compression, evaluated against clean ground truth at Vid4 spatial ×4 and temporal ×2. The retained main benchmark protocols are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds learned-frequency analysis (Section 4.4/Figure 6), controlled basis-capacity, frequency-learning and training-duration ablations (Table 8), and corruption robustness tests (Table 9). Figure 13 also examines a motion-blurred example. These substantially extend v1's model-scaling and temporal-consistency analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new frequency histograms and corruption-noise standard deviations do not represent experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial baseline, ablation, corruption and qualitative results. Existing values also change under the same reported settings: V3's Adobe240 Average becomes 32.29/0.917 from 32.24/0.916 in Table 1; its VFI result becomes 33.43/0.936 from 33.31/0.935 in Table 3; and tOF becomes 0.254 from 0.257. Table 2's V3 scores and Table 3's VideoINR scores also change. These revisions are not explained as a documented method or protocol change.

T1.justification: The mathematical representation and Equations 1–4 are retained, apart from notation and punctuation corrections. Additional Nyquist/PSF explanations and discussion of fixed-basis capacity introduce no substantive new formal definition, derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same claims: a unified continuous Fourier video representation, arbitrary spatial/temporal sampling, improved reconstruction and greater computational efficiency. Added experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets learned frequency concentrations as adaptation to video structure and fine-detail reconstruction. Appendix B.3 explains fixed-basis weakness through sparse frequency allocation and motivates 512 functions as a capacity compromise. The existing limitations concerning oversmoothing, finite representational capacity and broader degradations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the L1 reconstruction loss, describes the 256-dimensional encoder-output mapping used in ablations, and documents corruption generation through normalization, noise addition, 8-bit rounding and compression. Figure 14 explains the unavailable B-AVSR checkpoint. Existing hardware, optimizer and project-access information is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for CLIT, HIIF, BasicVSR, TTVSR, FTVSR and the signal-processing textbook, and expands discussion of AISR generations and specialized VSR competitors. The central novelty positioning and related-work section remain largely unchanged. Thera's publication update is bibliographic maintenance.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. v2 expands selected PSF and baseline explanations, subdivides Appendix B, moves computational complexity into Section 4.5, and updates the conference header. These are limited editorial and organizational changes rather than a pervasive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds the frequency-analysis visualization, two qualitative comparison figures and three substantive tables covering VSR comparisons, ablations and corruptions. Table 2 gains the HIIF row, and the existing computational table moves into the main text. Most earlier qualitative figures are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification: Table 8 directly tests basis design and training-budget choices that v1 mainly supported through benchmark performance and intuition, while Table 9 establishes behavior under input corruption. Broader comparisons and loss disclosure further improve evaluation and reproducibility. Table 7's unspecified evaluation dataset and missing H.264 settings limit some additions, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation.
